prize_parts.citation: for credibly identified evidence on how import competition reshapes local labour markets, employment and earnings

statement.case_for: My preferred part and names are unchanged from round 1: a single part, B044, with Autor, Dorn and Hanson. Two things changed. First, I have narrowed the citation to the trade-shock evidence and local labour-market adjustment, as the chair's questions invited. The three credited names jointly wrote the central papers, so this is where attribution is cleanest. It also avoids implying that these three own the task-based framework, whose lineage runs through Levy, Murnane, Katz and Acemoglu. Second, I now list B040 as my first alternative, in place of B024, because the round-1 exchange convinced me it is the strongest competing case. On merit, the China-shock design turned a first-order question, who bears the costs of trade integration and how labour markets adjust, into transparent quasi-experimental evidence. The result is that displacement is concentrated, large and persistent, and the gains are unevenly shared. It has been replicated in other countries and data sets, and a decade or more of scrutiny has refined magnitudes without overturning the qualitative finding. It also changed trade and labour economics and the policy debate. The criteria I weigh are influence, durability, credible identification and clean attribution. I do not use the four-four split between B040 and B044 as evidence of merit in either direction.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged. This is a research design and a body of empirical findings, not a single conceptual breakthrough, and a committee that puts conceptual generality first could reasonably prefer B040. The shift-share and instrumental-variable inference is delicate, and the size and persistence of the effects are contested. Part of that debate is how much is trade and how much is automation. The trade-shock papers date from about 2013, so they have a shorter record than Kiyotaki-Moore (1997), and I accept that this is a real maturity difference. The narrowed citation also leaves the task and skill-bias literature unrecognised in this part, which some will see as only half of the technology-and-inequality story. B040 has the cleaner two-person attribution, and I cannot settle from the files how much the 2022 prize narrows its marginal case. My field proximity is a further risk. I work in empirical labour economics and design-based evaluation, and I may over-weight direct identification relative to conceptual mechanisms, so I have tried to state the maturity and validation points against my own preference.

responses.point: Hassler prefers B040 and lists B044 as his first alternative, with Autor and Hanson only. He regards the task and trade-shock strands as separable and says Dorn would be omitted from the central China-shock papers. He also says his reservation about B044 would weaken considerably if the committee anchors on the trade-shock evidence.
responses.response: I have taken that route. The citation now rests on import competition and local labour-market adjustment alone, which is the condition he set. His own reasoning then supports including Dorn. If the achievement is the China-shock design, omitting one of its three joint authors is the attribution error he identified, and the three-name cap does not force it. I concede his maturity point: a 1997 mechanism has had nearly thirty years of scrutiny and the 2013 papers have had about thirteen. I do not think that gap disqualifies B044 when the test is whether the core finding survived replication and re-estimation. I also accept his refinement that Gertler and Gilchrist should be excluded on the independent origin of the collateral-constraint mechanism and not on prior recognition. That removes one argument against B040 that I might otherwise have leaned on.

responses.point: Andersson prefers B040 as a clean two-person conceptual mechanism and ranked B044 eighth. In round 1 he said that rank was probably too low, but he kept B044 as an alternative because the task and trade-shock strands may be two contributions, and Dorn is a core author of the second.
responses.response: His stated hesitation was that the committee should settle which strand it is crediting before it settles names. The narrowed citation answers that. It credits one strand, with Autor, Dorn and Hanson as its joint authors. I agree that B040 has the cleaner attribution and the longer record. We differ on how to weigh indirect validation against shift-share inference concerns. He treats the mixed empirical validation of Kiyotaki-Moore as a real but common weakness of foundational mechanisms. I treat the inference debate on the China shock as a real weakness too, but one that bears on magnitudes more than on the qualitative result. I may be biased towards direct evidence, and I do not claim the disagreement is resolved. I keep B040 as my first alternative for these reasons.

responses.point: Dreber-Almenberg describes my round-1 proposal as dropping Dorn. She says known inference problems in shift-share designs bear on the effect sizes the policy argument relies on. She also says she would accept B044 as a close alternative if the committee settles the two-strand question.
responses.response: The Dorn point is out of date. I moved to Autor, Dorn and Hanson during round 1, and my opening pair was a misattribution. On inference, she is right that the policy argument leans on magnitudes. But she proposes that the B040 citation should claim the mechanism and its influence, not its quantitative size. The same standard applies here. My citation claims credibly identified evidence of concentrated, persistent local labour-market adjustment costs, and it does not claim a precise elasticity or an exact trade-versus-automation split. The papers' qualitative result has survived re-examination of persistence and inference. I accept the timing difference she raises and I do not claim a cleaner attribution than B040. On the two-strand question, I now treat it as settled by the narrower citation.

responses.point: Krusell now prefers B044 with Autor, Dorn and Hanson, and he anchors the citation on trade-shock evidence, not the task-based theory. He identifies shift-share inference as the main scientific reservation and the trade-versus-automation question as unsettled. He also concedes that B040 has a cleaner, older and more conceptual claim.
responses.response: I agree with his anchoring and I have adopted it. My earlier citation referred to both import competition and technological change, which gave the task lineage more credit than these three names can carry. I also share his view that apportioning labour-market change between trade and automation is not settled. That is why I now name import competition only. Where I differ slightly is that I do not accept the characterisation of the contribution as only empirical application. A design that changed how a field measures adjustment costs is a methodological and conceptual change in what the profession counts as evidence. But I accept his point that a committee which weights theory-driven mechanisms first can legitimately prefer B040, and I do not think that is an unreasonable criterion.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson prefers B044 with Autor, Hanson and Dorn after dropping Katz. She treats the effect-size debate as concerning size and persistence and not the existence of adjustment costs. She also names the citation question as open: whether it holds the framework and the evidence together without overstating what the three names did on tasks.
responses.response: I agree with her on the names and on the nature of the debate. On her citation question, I resolve it differently from my own round-1 wording. A citation covering both technology and trade invites the overstatement she warns about, since the task lineage includes Katz and Levy-Murnane and Acemoglu is already a laureate. My narrower wording avoids that, at the price of leaving the skill-bias and task literature to separate recognition. I accept that price. Her case for B044 over B040 rests partly on the direct identification of the evidence. I weigh that too, but it is one criterion among several, and I do not want to count it as decisive against B040's clean two-person attribution.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the narrowed trade-shock citation as one prize-sized achievement, or still see it as a research design without enough conceptual weight against a mechanism such as B040.
Whether roughly thirteen years of replication is enough maturity for the China-shock work when B040 and other candidates have two to three decades.
How large and persistent the effects are under alternative inference methods for shift-share designs, and how much of the local labour-market adjustment is trade and how much is automation.
Whether leaving the task and skill-bias literature, including Katz, outside this part is the right call, or whether the committee would want a version that credits that strand.
How much the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises narrows B040's marginal case. I cannot settle this from the files and I have not independently verified any member's description of that overlap.
Whether the 2024 institutions prize or other recent labour-related prizes affect timing for B044. I do not think they decide it, but others may.
statement.conflict_note: No co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Katz, Kiyotaki, Moore, Chetty or Hendren is apparent from my supplied profile. My listed co-authors (Holmlund, Edin, Åslund, Öckert, Johansson, Nybom, Oosterbeek, van Ours and others) are not credited on any shortlisted ballot. I disclose field proximity: my research is in empirical labour economics and design-based evaluation, close to B044. I also gave the 2021 presentation speech as chair, praising natural-experiment methods, and that may predispose me towards quasi-experimental evidence. I have tried to apply the common criteria and have stated B044's weaknesses against B040. These are disclosures and are not adjudicated.
